blocks.text: Memory only holds numbers. So every character is stored as a **number** — its **code** — and a string is a row of those numbers sitting next to each other in memory. Which number each character gets, and how many bytes it takes, is decided by an **encoding**.

The oldest encoding still in daily use, **ASCII**, gives 128 characters the numbers 0 to 127 — enough for English letters, digits, punctuation and a few control characters. Each one fits in a single byte. The ranges are worth remembering:

items: **Lowercase** `'a'`–`'z'` are 97–122 — exactly 32 more than the uppercase letter.

blocks.alt: The string Cat! as four boxes C, a, t and !. Under each is its ASCII code: 67, 97, 116 and 33. Under that, the memory address of each byte: 1000, 1001, 1002 and 1003, one byte after another.

blocks.text: Character arithmetic: the trick behind many solutions

Because letters are consecutive numbers, you can do arithmetic on them. `ch - 'a'` turns `'a'` into 0, `'b'` into 1, … `'z'` into 25 — a ready-made **array index**. `ch - '0'` turns the digit character `'7'` into the number 7. And `'a' <= ch && ch <= 'z'` checks for a lowercase letter without any library call.
When a question says *"s consists of lowercase English letters"*, it is quietly inviting you to replace a hash map with an array of **26 counts**: faster, smaller, and always O(1) space.

blocks.caption: Each letter's code minus the code of 'a' says which of the 26 counters to add one to.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** The array always has 26 slots, however long the string is. In JavaScript and Python a character is a one-letter string, so you ask for its code (`charCodeAt`, `ord`); in Java and C++ a `char` already *is* a number.
Unicode and UTF-8: every character in every language

128 characters can't hold é, ü, अ, 中 or 😀. **Unicode** gives every character in every writing system its own number, called a **code point** — written like `U+00E9` for é. There's room for over a million.

**UTF-8**, the encoding of almost every web page and file today, stores each code point in **1 to 4 bytes**. Plain ASCII characters still take one byte, so English text looks exactly as it did in ASCII. Accented Latin letters take 2 bytes, most other scripts 3, and emoji 4.

blocks.alt: Four characters and their UTF-8 bytes. a is U+0061 and takes 1 byte, 61. é is U+00E9 and takes 2 bytes, C3 A9. The euro sign is U+20AC and takes 3 bytes, E2 82 AC. The grinning face emoji is U+1F600 and takes 4 bytes, F0 9F 98 80.

blocks.text: Each language counts in its own unit, which is why the "same" string can have different lengths:

blocks.code:
"cat"   "é"   "😀"
JavaScript         3      1     2     UTF-16 code units
Java               3      1     2     UTF-16 code units
Python             3      1     1     code points
C++ std::string    3      2     4     bytes (UTF-8 source)

blocks.text: JavaScript and Java store text as **UTF-16**, where most characters take one 16-bit unit but emoji take two — so `"😀".length` is 2. Python counts **code points**. A C++ `std::string` is just bytes. For interview questions limited to English letters all four agree; when emoji or accents are involved, loop by code point (`for...of` in JavaScript, `codePoints()` in Java).
How a string object sits in memory

Under the hood a string is a small **object** that knows its length, pointing at a contiguous block of character data. That's why reading the length is O(1) in every language here, and `s[i]` is O(1) too.

blocks.alt: Left: a string object with three fields, length 5, a cached hash, and a pointer to the characters. The pointer leads to five boxes, h e l l o, stored next to each other at addresses 2000 to 2004. Right: a C string, the same five characters followed by a zero byte that marks the end.

elements.text: C: no length field, a zero byte marks the end

items: **Java** keeps a `byte[]` plus a flag: one byte per character when every character fits in Latin-1, otherwise two (UTF-16). The hash code is cached after the first `hashCode()` call.
**Python** picks 1, 2 or 4 bytes per character for the whole string, based on its widest character, so `s[i]` stays O(1).
**C++** `std::string` stores a pointer, a size and a capacity — and keeps short strings (around 15 characters) inside the object itself, avoiding a separate allocation.
**C** has no string type at all: a `char` array ending in a zero byte. Finding the length means walking to that zero.
**"Lowercase English letters"** — use an `int[26]` indexed by `ch - 'a'`.
**"ASCII characters"** — use an `int[128]` (or 256) indexed by the code itself.
**Any character at all** — use a hash map keyed by the character.
**Length and indexing are O(1)**, so `for (i = 0; i < s.length; i++)` costs nothing extra per step.
